# How the World’s Wealthiest Governments Invest

The governments with the greatest investable public financial assets are not necessarily the countries with the largest economies. On a broad measure that includes central-bank reserves, sovereign wealth funds and public pension assets, the leading government investors are China’s People’s Bank of China and SAFE Investment Company, Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, Japan’s GPIF and China Investment Corporation. Among the requested sovereign wealth funds, Norway, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, Singapore, Saudi Arabia and Qatar are the central cases, but their strategies differ sharply.

Their common pattern is long-term diversification, rising exposure to private markets and growing use of direct investment and co-investment. Their main differences arise from purpose: Norway and Kuwait primarily save resource wealth for future generations; Japan invests pension reserves; Singapore manages reserves through distinct institutions; China separates reserve management from overseas and domestic state-capital platforms; while Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Qatar increasingly combine financial returns with economic diversification, industrial policy and strategic influence. The strongest evidence does not support a single ranking of “wealthiest governments,” because reported assets are measured at different dates and may include overlapping or consolidated state entities.

## Roadmap

The report first defines the investable-assets measure and explains why it differs from GDP, public net wealth and private national wealth. It then profiles the principal vehicles in Norway, China, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Kuwait and Qatar; compares what they own and how they invest; explains their fiscal, pension, stabilization, development and strategic purposes; evaluates governance and risk; and finally compares returns and strategic changes over time.

## 1. Who counts as the world’s wealthiest governments?

### A practical definition of government wealth

For investment comparison, the most useful definition is the value of financial assets controlled by the state through an identifiable investment vehicle. This includes:

- sovereign wealth funds and reserve-investment corporations;
- public pension and pension-reserve funds;
- central-bank reserve portfolios and official foreign-exchange assets;
- strategic or development investment funds; and
- state holding companies where reported assets include operating subsidiaries.

This is an institutional measure, not a measure of the total wealth of a country. It asks: how much capital can a government-controlled institution invest, and what type of capital is it?

That definition is broader than the Santiago Principles definition of a sovereign wealth fund, which focuses on a government-owned special-purpose investment fund created for macroeconomic purposes and using strategies that include foreign financial assets. The International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds excludes central-bank foreign-currency reserves from its database, including the reserves managed by China’s SAFE and Saudi Arabia’s monetary authority. It also warns that revisions and methodology changes limit year-to-year comparability ([IFSWF data project](https://www.ifswf.org/ifswfs-data-project)).

A broad government-investor ranking is therefore useful for identifying the largest pools of state-controlled capital, but it must not be read as a clean ranking of national wealth or even as a country-by-country total.

### The broadest current ranking

Global SWF’s September 2026 ranking orders government investors by the latest available assets under management in US dollars, using estimates when current disclosure is unavailable. It labels entities as sovereign wealth funds, public pension funds, central banks or reserve-fund organizations. On that basis, the leading entries are:

| Rank | Investor | Country | Type | Reported AUM |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | People’s Bank of China | China | Central bank | $3.883 trillion |
| 2 | Norges Bank Investment Management | Norway | Sovereign fund | $2.284 trillion |
| 3 | SAFE Investment Company | China | Sovereign fund/reserve investor | $2.047 trillion |
| 4 | Government Pension Investment Fund | Japan | Public pension fund | $1.962 trillion |
| 5 | China Investment Corporation | China | Sovereign fund | $1.567 trillion |

These are latest-period figures rather than a common-date observation. The PBoC and SAFE figures concern reserve-management institutions, while GPIF is a pension investor and NBIM manages Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global. The ranking therefore answers the question “which government-controlled investment entities are largest?” rather than “which countries have the most net public wealth?” ([Global SWF ranking](https://globalswf.com/ranking)).

The same table reports the following figures for several requested institutions:

| Investor | Reported AUM | Reported alternatives | Reported domestic exposure |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GIC | $1.161 trillion | 39% | 0% |
| Kuwait Investment Authority | $1.002 trillion | 25% | 6% |
| Abu Dhabi Investment Authority | $1.128 trillion | 35% | 0% |
| Public Investment Fund | $906 billion | 55% | 80% |
| Qatar Investment Authority | $580 billion | 45% | 35% |
| Temasek | $401 billion | 50% | 27% |
| Mubadala | $385 billion | 65% | 23% |

The “alternatives” category in this ranking combines real estate, infrastructure, private equity and hedge funds. It therefore does not show how much is in each of those categories, nor whether a percentage is a strategic target or a realized allocation. The domestic percentages also depend on how subsidiaries and operating companies are classified.

A separate 2026 ranking by Sovereign Wealth Research and IE University uses a more focused sovereign-fund universe. It counted 109 funds with combined AUM of $15.1 trillion in April 2026, compared with 104 funds and $13.2 trillion in its 2024 edition. It attributes about half of the increase to organic growth, with the rest reflecting new entrants and methodological changes. Asia-Pacific and the Middle East together accounted for roughly 79% of global sovereign AUM; Europe accounted for 16%, with Norway’s GPFG representing about 85% of the European total ([Sovereign Wealth Funds 2026 report](https://www.investinspain.org/content/dam/icex-invest/documentos/publicaciones/publicaciones_eng/swf-2026.pdf)).

Its leading entries were:

| Rank | Vehicle | Country | AUM |
|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Government Pension Fund Global | Norway | $2.100 trillion |
| 2 | State Administration of Foreign Exchange | China | $1.988 trillion |
| 3 | China Investment Corporation | China | $1.570 trillion |
| 4 | Abu Dhabi Investment Authority | UAE | $1.187 trillion |
| 5 | Kuwait Investment Authority | Kuwait | $1.002 trillion |
| 6 | GIC | Singapore | $936 billion |
| 7 | Public Investment Fund | Saudi Arabia | $913 billion |
| 8 | Qatar Investment Authority | Qatar | $580 billion |
| 9 | Hong Kong Monetary Authority Exchange Fund | Hong Kong | $533 billion |
| 10 | Saudi monetary-authority reserves | Saudi Arabia | $430 billion |

This ranking is not directly interchangeable with the Global SWF table. It includes quasi-sovereign reserve investors and uses different reporting dates and perimeters. It also distinguishes between financial-portfolio funds, whose AUM reflects the market value of investments, and holding or strategic funds, whose AUM may include consolidated operating subsidiaries. The report explicitly says those categories are not directly comparable.

### Why China illustrates the measurement problem

China shows why government-investor rankings cannot simply be added together.

CIC reports total assets of $1.57 trillion and net assets of $1.37 trillion at the end of 2024. It was created in 2007 to diversify China’s foreign-exchange holdings and was initially capitalized with $200 billion in reserves purchased from the PBoC in exchange for RMB1.55 trillion in Ministry of Finance bonds. A later $50 billion injection went to CIC International ([CIC assessment](https://www.ifswf.org/assessment/cic-2025); [CIC 2024 results](https://www.china-inv.cn/chinainven/Media/2025-12/1002912.shtml)).

SAFE’s official statistics, by contrast, report China’s external portfolio investment assets excluding reserve assets at $1.9875 trillion at the end of 2025. That total contained $1.2628 trillion of equity and $724.7 billion of bonds. But the figures cover resident sectors rather than a single government vehicle: non-bank financial institutions held 56%, banks 29% and the non-financial sector 16%. The total therefore cannot be treated as SAFE Investment Company’s AUM or as entirely government-owned ([SAFE external portfolio statistics](https://www.safe.gov.cn/en/2026/0529/2419.html)).

China’s full International Investment Position adds another layer. At the end of 2025, China reported external financial assets of $11.786 trillion, liabilities of $7.715 trillion and net external assets of $4.071 trillion. Reserve assets were $3.744 trillion, while direct investment, portfolio investment and other investment accounted for the rest. This is a national external balance-sheet measure, not a sovereign-fund measure ([SAFE International Investment Position](https://www.safe.gov.cn/en/2026/0327/2405.html)).

The correct conclusion is not that one of these figures is “the true Chinese wealth figure.” They measure different layers:

1. central-bank and official-reserve assets;
2. a state-owned reserve-diversification corporation;
3. resident-sector external assets; and
4. the entire national external balance sheet.

Without an unduplicated country-level reconciliation, they should not be summed.

### AUM, GDP, public net wealth and national wealth are different rankings

A country can be rich under one measure and comparatively weak under another.

#### GDP

GDP measures annual economic production. It says how large an economy is, not how much financial capital its government controls. A large economy may have substantial public debt, limited sovereign-fund assets and a negative net financial position. A smaller resource-exporting economy may have a sovereign fund worth a large multiple of GDP.

The supplied evidence does not provide a complete GDP ranking alongside government-investor AUM, so an exact alternate ordering should not be manufactured. The useful analytical point is that GDP and investable public assets answer different questions.

#### General-government net financial worth

The OECD defines general-government net financial worth as financial assets minus outstanding liabilities for central, state and local governments and social-security funds. It is expressed as a percentage of GDP and excludes nonfinancial public assets. The OECD’s 2022 chart covered 37 countries ranging from -138.98% to 253.47% of GDP, illustrating the wide difference between governments’ financial positions ([OECD general-government financial wealth](https://www.oecd.org/en/data/indicators/general-government-financial-wealth.html)).

This measure includes debt, pension liabilities, deposits, loans, equities and other financial claims. A government can therefore have a large sovereign fund but lower net financial wealth if its liabilities are also large.

#### Public-sector net worth

The IMF’s public-sector balance-sheet approach includes financial and nonfinancial public assets and liabilities, including public corporations. Its database for 38 countries found total public-sector assets of $103 trillion, liabilities of $93 trillion and net worth of $10 trillion, or 21% of GDP. General-government debt accounted for $44 trillion and current pension obligations for $22 trillion ([IMF public wealth balance sheets](https://blog-pfm.imf.org/en/pfmblog/2019/06/a-global-picture-of-public-wealth)).

Public-sector net worth is closer to a government balance-sheet concept than to an investment-fund ranking. It includes infrastructure, land, state-owned enterprises and public pension obligations. It may therefore rank a government with substantial public infrastructure differently from one with a large liquid sovereign fund.

#### Private or broader national wealth

Private national wealth includes households, corporations and privately owned real estate and financial assets. It may be enormous even when the state has few investable assets. Conversely, a government may control a large sovereign fund in a country whose private household wealth is much smaller.

The supplied evidence does not provide a comparable global ranking of private national wealth. That field therefore remains unavailable here. It should not be substituted with AUM.

### The selection used in this report

The practical selection rule is:

- use the broad government-controlled investable-asset ranking to identify the largest entities;
- distinguish strict sovereign funds from central banks, reserve managers and public pensions;
- profile the seven requested countries and their principal vehicles;
- avoid adding vehicles that may overlap; and
- report estimates, dates and measurement limitations beside each figure.

Under this rule, Japan’s GPIF, China’s PBoC and SAFE, Hong Kong’s Exchange Fund, Korea Investment Corporation, Indonesia’s Danantara, Australia’s Future Fund and Saudi Arabia’s monetary reserves are relevant leading government investors even though they are not all conventional sovereign wealth funds.

## 2. Profiles of leading government investment institutions

### The main institutional types

Governments invest through several distinct vehicles. Their funding source and liability structure usually explain more about their portfolios than the generic label “sovereign wealth fund.”

| Vehicle type | Typical funding | Main purpose | Liquidity tendency | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stabilization fund | Commodity or fiscal surpluses | Smooth budget and economic shocks | High liquidity, lower risk | Kuwait GRF, Ireland ICNF |
| Savings or intergenerational fund | Resource revenue or fiscal surpluses | Preserve wealth for future generations | Long horizon, greater illiquidity | Norway GPFG, Kuwait FGF, QIA |
| Pension-reserve fund | Pension contributions and reserves | Support future pension liabilities | Long horizon but benefit-liquidity needs | Japan GPIF |
| Reserve-investment corporation | Foreign-exchange reserves | Improve returns while preserving external purchasing power | Liquid core with some alternatives | CIC, GIC |
| Strategic or development fund | State transfers, assets or borrowing | Diversification, infrastructure and industrial policy | Flexible, often domestic and illiquid | PIF, Mubadala, ADQ, Temasek |

The IMF uses a similar typology of stabilization funds, savings funds, pension-reserve funds and reserve-investment corporations. Some institutions have multiple objectives, as do Kuwait’s KIA and Norway’s GPFG ([IMF sovereign-fund classification](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/display/book/9781589069275/CH011.xml)).

### Norway: GPFG as a transparent global savings portfolio

Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global is the clearest example of a resource-savings vehicle designed to transform temporary oil income into permanent financial capital. The fund was established in 1990 after the discovery and development of North Sea oil, with capital transfers beginning later. Its policy purpose is to preserve wealth for future generations while allowing the budget to use only the expected real return. Norway’s fiscal rule was initially based on a 4% expected real return and was revised to 3% in 2017 ([Sovereign Wealth Funds 2026 report](https://www.investinspain.org/content/dam/icex-invest/documentos/publicaciones/publicaciones_eng/swf-2026.pdf)).

The fund is owned by the Norwegian people, represented by the government and the Storting. The Ministry of Finance holds formal responsibility and sets the mandate, while Norges Bank Investment Management executes the investment management within that mandate ([NBIM 2025 annual report](https://www.nbim.no/contentassets/6db259ec684645ebbf171cacbe7cc7de/annual-report-2025.pdf)).

At the end of 2025, the GPFG’s fund value was NOK21,268 billion. Its investment portfolio comprised:

- 71.3% equities;
- 26.5% fixed income;
- 1.7% unlisted real estate; and
- 0.4% unlisted renewable-energy infrastructure.

The investment-portfolio market value was NOK21,286 billion. The difference reflects deferred tax and accrued management fees included in the wider fund-value calculation.

The GPFG is almost entirely foreign-facing. Its equity portfolio in the first half of 2025 was 57.7% North America, 22.2% Europe, 10.5% Asia and Oceania and 10.8% emerging markets. At the end of 2025 it held investments across 68 countries and 34 currencies, including 7,201 listed companies and 7,600 bonds from 1,618 issuers ([GPFG half-year report](https://www.nbim.no/contentassets/4929094bc7f0436c8d311e10557f8b83/gpfg-half-year-report-2025.pdf); [NBIM 2025 annual report](https://www.nbim.no/en/news-and-insights/reports/2025/annual-report-2025/)).

Its benchmark is a public-market reference portfolio, principally 70% equities and 30% fixed income. The fund is managed close to that benchmark, but every investment process has active elements. Security selection, internal and external management and limited unlisted exposure are intended to add diversification or excess return.

Norway’s approach is distinctive because the fiscal and investment roles are separated. The fund is not a domestic industrial-policy vehicle. NBIM’s practice is not to invest in Norway, and the fund’s formal objective is the highest possible return after costs at acceptable risk, subject to responsible-management requirements.

### China: a multi-vehicle state balance sheet

China does not have one sovereign investor. It has a layered system in which the central bank, foreign-exchange authority, sovereign investment corporation and domestic state-financial-capital steward perform different functions.

#### PBoC and SAFE

The People’s Bank of China and SAFE are reserve-management authorities. SAFE Investment Company operates and manages official foreign-exchange and gold reserves and invests internationally in bonds, equities and alternative assets through overseas subsidiaries ([Global SWF profile](https://globalswf.com/fund/PBOC)).

The PBoC’s $3.883 trillion entry in the broad Global SWF ranking is a central-bank measure. It should not be compared directly with CIC’s net assets or with China’s entire external portfolio. The supplied evidence does not provide a complete vehicle-level asset allocation, governance structure, benchmark, return series or risk statistics for PBoC or SAFE Investment Company. Those fields remain unavailable.

#### CIC and Central Huijin

CIC was established in 2007 to diversify China’s foreign-exchange holdings and seek maximum returns within acceptable risk. It describes itself as a financial investor that does not seek control of portfolio companies. Its domestic subsidiary, Central Huijin, separately holds stakes in Chinese state-owned financial institutions.

CIC’s portfolio framework distinguishes:

1. a reference portfolio;
2. a policy portfolio; and
3. an actual portfolio.

CIC says total returns are determined by reference-portfolio selection, policy-portfolio construction and actual portfolio management. The portfolio spans public equities, fixed income, alternative assets and cash products. Overseas activities through CIC International and CIC Capital include public equities and bonds, hedge funds, multi-asset strategies, private equity, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, resources, commodities and agriculture ([CIC portfolio management](http://www.china-inv.cn/chinainven/Investments/Portfolio_Management.shtml); [CIC 2023 annual report](https://www.china-inv.cn/chinainven/xhtml/Media/2023EN.pdf)).

At the end of 2024, CIC reported total assets of $1.57 trillion and net assets of $1.37 trillion. Central Huijin’s state-owned financial capital under stewardship was reported at CNY6.87 trillion. CIC’s 10-year annualized cumulative net return was 6.92% in US dollars, 61 basis points above its 10-year performance target. The source does not name a conventional market benchmark and does not report a comparable volatility or drawdown series.

CIC’s 2025 Santiago Principles self-assessment describes an 11-member board with three executive directors, five non-executive directors, two independent directors and one employee director. It reports annual reports, audited consolidated statements, conflict-of-interest rules and a risk framework covering market, liquidity, country, geopolitical, cybersecurity, compliance and climate risks. These are self-reported governance claims rather than an independent external evaluation ([CIC Santiago assessment](https://www.ifswf.org/assessment/cic-2025)).

### The United Arab Emirates: three Abu Dhabi models

Abu Dhabi has several state-controlled investors with distinct functions. ADIA is a global savings portfolio; Mubadala combines commercial investing with national industrial development; ADQ is a more domestic developmental holding platform. MGX adds a specialized artificial-intelligence vehicle.

#### ADIA: global diversification and limited disclosure

ADIA was established in 1976 to invest funds on behalf of the Government of Abu Dhabi. Its mission is to sustain Abu Dhabi’s long-term prosperity by prudently growing capital through a disciplined process. It does not publicly disclose AUM or holdings. External estimates range from roughly $1 trillion to $1.187 trillion, depending on date and methodology ([ADIA](https://www.adia.ae/); [ADIA 2025 review](https://www.adia.ae/en/pr/2025a/pdf/adia-annual-review-2025_final.pdf)).

Its published long-term strategy portfolio provides ranges rather than realized weights:

| ADIA strategy range | Minimum | Maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| Developed-market equities | 32% | 42% |
| Emerging-market equities | 7% | 15% |
| Small-cap equities | 1% | 5% |
| Government bonds | 7% | 15% |
| Credit | 2% | 7% |
| Financial alternatives | 5% | 10% |
| Real estate | 5% | 10% |
| Private equity | 12% | 17% |
| Infrastructure | 2% | 7% |
| Cash | 0% | 5% |

Financial alternatives comprise hedge funds and managed futures. The ranges are intentionally flexible and do not represent a single actual allocation.

ADIA’s 2025 review increased the financial-alternatives range from 5–10% to 7–12% and private equity from 12–17% to 15–20%, while lowering the real-estate range from 5–10% to 2–7%. ADIA said the lower real-estate range did not imply a fall in absolute real-estate exposure.

Its displayed geographic ranges allocate 45–60% to North America, 15–30% to Europe, 5–10% to developed Asia and 10–20% to emerging markets. The same page also contains a second descriptive set of ranges—35–50%, 20–35%, 10–20% and 15–25%. The source does not explain which set is authoritative, so the geographic figures should be treated as conflicting published ranges rather than a precise actual allocation.

ADIA states that, as a matter of practice, it does not invest in the UAE. Its investment approach is therefore one of the most externally oriented among the major Gulf funds. In 2025, 57% of the portfolio was reported as internally managed and 43% externally managed; 63% was classified as active management and 37% as index replication. ADIA’s Private Equities Department uses direct investments, funds, platforms, structured financing, GP-led secondaries and co-investment partnerships.

ADIA’s 20-year annualized return at the end of 2025 was 6.6% and its 30-year annualized return was 7.2%. The figures were calculated on a time-weighted basis from audited financial data, but 2025 results remained provisional pending final data for non-listed assets. No named market benchmark is supplied in the cited disclosure.

#### Mubadala: commercial returns with a domestic transformation role

Mubadala’s mandate is to deliver sustainable risk-adjusted returns for the Government of Abu Dhabi. It invests globally, but its domestic role is explicitly developmental: creating national champions, high-value jobs and competitive industries. Its named sectors include energy, advanced technology, infrastructure, healthcare, consumer businesses and private credit ([Mubadala strategy](https://annual2024.mubadala.com/our-strategy); [Mubadala 2025 annual review](https://annual2025.mubadala.com/en)).

Mubadala reported 2025 assets of AED1.4 trillion, approximately $385 billion, up 17% year on year. It reported a 10.7% five-year annualized return and a 10.3% 10-year annualized return. The company has published rolling IRR rather than annual revenue and net-income figures since 2021, reflecting its preference for long-horizon performance measures ([Mubadala 2025 results](https://www.mubadala.com/en/news/strong-performance-by-uae-portfolio-drives-mubadalas-growth-in-2025)).

A company-reported 2025 portfolio breakdown, reproduced by Caproasia, was:

- 42% private markets;
- 20% public markets;
- 17% real estate and infrastructure;
- 16% alternatives; and
- 5% credit.

Geographic exposure was reported as 44% North America, 24% UAE, 15% Europe, 13% Asia-Pacific and 1% Latin America. Those figures sum to 97%; the source does not explain the remaining 3%, so the geographic breakdown is incomplete ([Mubadala allocation and performance](https://www.caproasia.com/2026/04/16/uae-abu-dhabi-sovereign-wealth-fund-mubadala-investment-company-reports-385-billion-aum-in-2025-portfolio-return-10-7-5-year-irr-10-3-10-year-irr-portfolio-allocation-private-market-42-publi/)).

Mubadala’s direct arm is its largest investment arm and typically makes meaningful minority co-investments with selected partners. Its endowment arm, the Abu Dhabi Investment Council, uses a globally diversified portfolio mainly through asset managers. This combination gives Mubadala both direct influence and access to external-manager specialization.

The fund has also become a major investor in AI infrastructure, alternative credit, healthcare and life sciences. MGX, launched by Mubadala and Abu Dhabi technology group G42 in 2024, concentrates on AI, compute and data-center infrastructure. The IE report estimates MGX’s announced investment potential at roughly $50 billion, but explicitly warns that the figure includes third-party capital and debt mobilization rather than independently reported sovereign AUM ([Sovereign Wealth Funds 2026 report](https://www.investinspain.org/content/dam/icex-invest/documentos/publicaciones/publicaciones_eng/swf-2026.pdf)).

#### ADQ: domestic development and strategic holdings

ADQ, formally Abu Dhabi Developmental Holding Company, is more domestically oriented than ADIA and Mubadala. Bloomberg estimated its assets at $263 billion and found that more than one-third of approximately 280 transactions over the preceding five years involved UAE-based companies. The same analysis described ADQ as the fastest-growing of Abu Dhabi’s three major funds, with assets more than doubling over four years ([Bloomberg analysis](https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2025-abu-dhabi-investment-funds/)).

ADQ’s full mandate, actual asset allocation, regional and sector exposure, investment-method shares and benchmarked performance are not available in the supplied evidence. Its consolidated financial statements provide a useful but narrower data point: Level 3 fair-value financial assets were AED186.759 billion at the end of 2025, compared with AED137.960 billion in 2024. These are assets valued using unobservable inputs and are not equivalent to total AUM.

ADQ’s domestic orientation places it closer to a strategic holding and development platform than to a pure global reserve investor. That distinction matters because consolidated operating assets, infrastructure companies and domestic state holdings can make its headline asset figure look larger than a financial portfolio of listed securities.

### Saudi Arabia: PIF as a transformation engine

Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund was established in 1971 and reformed into the main financial engine of Vision 2030. Its statutory mandate is dual: generate returns and serve the public interest by promoting economic development, diversifying national income and protecting the interests of future generations ([PIF law](https://www.pif.gov.sa/-/media/project/pif-corporate/pif-corporate-site/our-investments/governance-and-investments/pdf/pif-law-documents-en11.pdf)).

Under the 2023 PIF Law, the fund has public legal personality and financial and administrative independence but reports to the Council of Economic and Development Affairs. Its board is chaired by the council’s president; other experts are appointed by royal order. PIF may invest in Saudi Arabia or abroad and may hold real estate, securities, currencies, commodities and derivatives. Its revenues may come from investment returns, state appropriations and borrowing.

PIF reported assets of SAR3.424 trillion at the end of 2024. Its 2025 annual report described more than $900 billion of AUM and cumulative domestic deployment above $199 billion during 2021–2025. It reported that its portfolio contributed 11% of Saudi non-oil GDP in 2025, although these development-contribution figures are PIF’s own attribution rather than independently standardized national-account measures ([PIF 2025 annual report](https://www.pif.gov.sa/en/annual-report-2025/)).

The portfolio is heavily domestic. Different sources report 76% Saudi Arabia, 20% international and 4% Treasury for a 2025 reporting basis, while another source reports 83% domestic and 17% international at the end of 2024. Those figures use different dates and perimeters. A secondary account reports 86% of management internally and 14% externally, but no official benchmark or volatility series accompanies the reported 5.8% annual return since 2017 ([PIF allocation and impact report](https://www.pif.gov.sa/-/media/project/pif-corporate/pif-corporate-site/our-financials/capital-markets-program/pdf/pif-allocation-impact-report-2025.pdf); [PIF portfolio summary](https://www.caproasia.com/2026/08/21/saudi-arabia-sovereign-wealth-fund-public-investment-fund-pif-reports-904-billion-aum-5-8-annual-return-since-2017-for-2025-portfolio-aum-saudi-arabia-76-international-20-treasury-4-investment-management-internal-86-external-14-sector-allocation-energy-28-real-estate-15-communication-10-it-9-financials-6-utilities-4-materials-5-industrials-4-consumer-discretionary-2-consumer-staples-1-healthcare-0-4-others-15-portfolio-allocation-saudi-equity-holdings-33-saudi-sector-development-29-saudi-real-estate-infrastructure-development-7-saudi-giga-projects-7-international-strategic-investment-10-international-diversified-pool-6-international-capital-markets-program-4-treasury-4-inv/)).

Reported 2025 allocation buckets were:

- 33% Saudi equity holdings;
- 29% Saudi sector development;
- 7% Saudi real-estate and infrastructure development;
- 7% Saudi giga-projects;
- 10% international strategic investment;
- 6% international diversified pool;
- 4% international capital-markets program; and
- 4% Treasury.

These are strategic portfolio buckets, not conventional asset classes. They show why PIF cannot be compared with GPFG simply by asking how much is in public equity or private equity.

Sector figures reproduced for 2025 put energy at 28%, real estate at 15%, communications at 10%, information technology at 9%, financials at 6%, materials at 5%, utilities and industrials at 4% each, consumer discretionary at 2%, consumer staples at 1%, healthcare at 0.4% and other sectors at 15%. The figures are reported with rounding and an undefined “other” category.

PIF’s distinctive investments include Saudi giga-projects, gaming and entertainment, Lucid Motors, Humain, digital infrastructure, tourism, financial services and industrial development. Its $55 billion Electronic Arts transaction in 2025 was a particularly large international strategic investment, while Humain connected PIF to Saudi AI infrastructure and partnerships with Google Cloud, AMD, Qualcomm and Nvidia. A reported $8 billion write-down of giga-project holdings in 2024 may reflect cost overruns, delays or revised expected returns; it does not by itself establish a retreat from diversification ([Oxford Economics analysis](https://www.oxfordeconomics.com/resource/saudi-arabias-pif-driving-diversification-through-strategic-investments/)).

PIF’s green-finance restrictions are narrower than a whole-portfolio ethical mandate. Its Green Finance Framework excludes certain activities from the use of green-bond proceeds, including power facilities above an emissions-intensity threshold of 100gCO2e/kWh, nuclear power generation and distribution assets, military activities, industrial agriculture and livestock practices. The restriction applies to eligible green-finance proceeds, not necessarily to the entire PIF portfolio.

### Singapore: a deliberately divided reserve system

Singapore separates three state-controlled institutions:

- GIC manages most government assets placed with it;
- the Monetary Authority of Singapore holds its own assets and manages the official foreign reserves; and
- Temasek is wholly owned by the government but owns the assets on its own balance sheet.

The Ministry of Finance sets overall mandates and objectives, ensures competent boards and reviews whole-portfolio performance and adverse scenarios. It says individual investment decisions remain with GIC and MAS management, while Temasek’s investment decisions are fully independent of government involvement or influence and its board has no government representation ([Singapore Ministry of Finance](https://www.mof.gov.sg/policies/reserves/who-manages-the-reserves/)).

#### GIC

GIC’s mandate is to preserve and enhance the international purchasing power of Singapore’s reserves by achieving long-term returns above global inflation. Its official AUM is not disclosed. Third-party estimates range from roughly $800 billion to $1.161 trillion, depending on source and date.

GIC organizes its portfolio into three broad groups—equities, fixed income and real assets—covering both public and private markets. It monitors regional exposure but does not allocate assets by geography as a primary portfolio-construction rule. A third-party summary of the year to March 2025 reported 51% equities, 26% fixed income and 23% real assets, with 49% in the Americas; those figures should be treated as an external estimate rather than a fully disclosed official AUM schedule ([GIC portfolio](https://www.gic.com.sg/our-portfolio/); [Altss ranking](https://altss.com/rankings/largest-sovereign-wealth-funds)).

GIC’s 65% global-equity/35% bond Reference Portfolio is not a performance benchmark. It is a risk reference and excludes investment costs. This distinction prevents a common mistake: comparing GIC’s actual portfolio return directly with a hypothetical 65/35 index as if GIC had promised to track it.

For the 20 years ending 31 March 2026, GIC reported a 5.6% annualized US-dollar nominal return and a 3.4% real return after global inflation. From the introduction of its New Investment Framework in April 2013 through March 2026, the portfolio grew at global inflation plus 4.2% per year, while active strategies contributed 52 basis points of gross alpha above the Policy Portfolio. The framework review that began in 2012 led to stronger private-market capabilities, value-creation expertise and strategic partnerships ([GIC 2025/26 annual report](https://www.gic.com.sg/uploads/2026/07/GIC_AR_2025-26_PRINT.pdf)).

GIC uses direct investment, co-investment, external managers and partnerships. It was involved in 12 transactions with other major sovereign funds during the July 2024–December 2025 period, more than any other fund in the IE dataset. Its investments span data centers, logistics, student housing, private credit, AI and healthcare.

#### Temasek

Temasek is an active, bottom-up equity investor rather than a reserve manager. Its portfolio includes Singapore-based companies, global direct investments and partnerships, funds and asset-management companies.

At 31 March 2025, Temasek reported a net portfolio value of S$434 billion. Its portfolio segments were 41% Singapore-based Temasek Portfolio Companies, 36% Global Direct Investments and 23% Partnerships, Funds and Asset Management Companies. Its 20-year Total Shareholder Return was 7% in Singapore-dollar terms and 8% in US-dollar terms; its 10-year return was 5% in both currency conventions ([Temasek 2025 results](https://www.temasek.com.sg/en/news-and-resources/news-room/news/2025/temasek-net-portfolio-value-grows-to-record-high-of-434-billion)).

Temasek reported S$518 billion of net portfolio value at 31 March 2026, but this is not directly equivalent to AUM reported by a financial-portfolio sovereign fund. It also does not operate against a conventional reference portfolio. The Singapore Ministry of Finance places it at the higher end of the risk spectrum relative to GIC because it invests directly in companies and does not manage toward a standard asset-allocation benchmark ([Singapore Ministry of Finance comparison](https://www.mof.gov.sg/news-resources/newsroom/overall-performance-management-of-temasek-holdings-and-gic/)).

Temasek uses partnerships and funds to scale exposure to private credit, hybrid solutions, private equity, hedge funds, closed-block insurance and royalties. It has also used Singapore portfolio companies such as Keppel, PSA, Sembcorp and SP Group to build infrastructure and industrial exposure.

Its climate targets are to reduce net carbon emissions attributable to the portfolio to half of 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050. These are portfolio objectives, not a restriction on every investment.

### Kuwait: the classic reserve-and-generations model

Kuwait’s investment system dates to the Kuwait Investment Board, established in 1953 to invest surplus oil revenues and reduce dependence on a finite resource. The Kuwait Investment Office replaced it in 1965, and the Kuwait Investment Authority was established in 1982 as the parent institution. A 1976 decree created the Future Generations Fund, requiring at least 10% of annual state revenues to be allocated to it ([KIA history](https://www.kia.gov.kw/about-kia/)).

KIA manages:

- the General Reserve Fund, which serves as the government’s treasury and investment arm;
- the Future Generations Fund, an intergenerational savings vehicle; and
- other funds entrusted by the Ministry of Finance.

The GRF consolidates state proceeds, helps finance government expenditure and can smooth fiscal and economic shocks. The FGF invests outside Kuwait across equities, bonds, private equity, real estate and infrastructure. Withdrawals from the FGF require legal authorization, and its income is reinvested by law.

KIA’s current AUM is not publicly disclosed. External estimates range from about $801 billion to $1.03 trillion, with the latter estimate placing it among the world’s largest sovereign funds. AGBI, citing S&P data, reported holdings across more than 90 companies and a company-geography distribution of 55% Middle East and Africa, 21% Asia-Pacific, 13% North America and 12% Europe. These are company-location figures, not a complete asset-allocation table ([AGBI analysis](https://www.agbi.com/analysis/finance/2025/06/the-kia-maintains-its-low-profile-approach-for-now/)).

KIA says it seeks to exceed composite benchmarks on a three-year rolling average through an uncorrelated asset allocation. It has a long horizon and tolerates short-term volatility. However, no realized return history, named composite benchmark values, volatility series or drawdown figures are available in the supplied evidence.

Its investments are mostly made through external fund managers. The Kuwait Investment Office in London invests directly in equities, fixed income and alternatives including infrastructure and real estate. KIA cannot borrow for investment or use derivative products, which imposes a more conservative implementation framework than some peers.

Governance is formally independent. KIA describes itself as an independent public authority whose board is responsible for long-term asset allocation and overall performance. Its accounts are externally audited and it submits semiannual AUM statements to the State Audit Bureau. Yet Kuwait’s Law No. 47 of 1982 restricts public disclosure of information related to KIA’s work and provides penalties for unauthorized disclosure. This makes KIA a strong example of the difference between accountability to state institutions and transparency to the public.

### Qatar: long-term savings with strategic deployment

Qatar Investment Authority was established in 2005. Its 2025 Santiago Principles self-assessment describes it as a governmental authority with legal personality and an independent budget, reporting to the Supreme Council for Economic Affairs and Investments, chaired by the Amir. It retains operational independence but its strategy is ultimately approved by the Supreme Council ([QIA Santiago assessment](https://www.ifswf.org/assessment/qia-2025)).

QIA invests Qatar’s fiscal surpluses for future generations. Its stated objectives are:

- long-term value creation;
- support for a competitive Qatari economy; and
- local stabilization when necessary.

The Supreme Council assigns funding in coordination with the Minister of Finance. QIA reinvests returns and reports no government asset withdrawals since inception, although emergency withdrawals remain legally possible by decision of the Amir.

QIA’s reported AUM varies materially by source and date: approximately $450 billion, $510 billion, $550 billion, $557 billion and $580 billion all appear in the supplied material. The $500 billion commitment announced for future US investment is a deployment pledge, not realized AUM. These figures should not be combined.

QIA introduced a formal top-down portfolio-allocation process in 2020. Its Reference Portfolio is intended to meet long-term return objectives within board-set risk and liquidity limits. Investment teams use internal management where QIA has expertise and external managers where appropriate. QIA also invests directly in real estate, private companies, pre-IPO rounds and public-market negotiated deals, and co-invests with external partners.

The fund has been especially active in AI, data centers, digital infrastructure, private credit, sports and entertainment. Its 2025 investment activity included the Anthropic and Databricks financings, xAI, robotics and quantum-computing companies, and a Brookfield-QIA AI infrastructure partnership. QIA also anchored a $200 million actively managed Qatar-equity fund with Fiera Capital to broaden local-market participation and liquidity ([QIA-Fiera partnership](https://qia.qa/en/Newsroom/Pages/QIA-and-Fiera-Capital-launch-USD-200m-Fiera-Equity-Fund--.aspx)).

QIA reports absolute returns for all portfolios and relative performance against approved benchmarks where appropriate. No named consolidated benchmark or numerical realized return is supplied in the cited evidence. Its actual asset-class, sector and regional percentages are also unavailable.

### Japan’s GPIF: a leading investor outside the sovereign-fund model

Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund belongs in the broad ranking because of its scale, but it is a pension reserve manager rather than a savings fund. Its legal mission is to manage pension reserves safely and efficiently over the long term for insured people. Japan’s pension system is principally pay-as-you-go, so GPIF’s reserve fund supplements future pension finance rather than directly matching each worker’s contributions to that worker’s benefits ([GPIF annual report](https://www.gpif.go.jp/en/performance/annual_report_fiscal_year_2024.pdf)).

Its fifth policy asset mix, effective April 2025, targets 25% each in domestic bonds, foreign bonds, domestic equities and foreign equities. At the end of March 2026, the actual pension-reserve allocation was 26.91% domestic bonds, 24.48% foreign bonds, 23.81% domestic equities and 24.80% foreign equities. Alternative investments represented 1.74% of the total, within a 5% ceiling.

GPIF uses both passive and active management, external managers and in-house management. Its FY2024 assets were 81.84% passive and 17.76% active, with the remainder in other assets. Alternative investments are implemented through funds of funds, external managers, co-investment arrangements and limited partnerships. The fund also uses futures and internal trading for rebalancing and liquidity.

For FY2025, GPIF returned 16.47% gross and reported cumulative returns of ¥196,930.6 billion since FY2001. The investment assets managed by GPIF itself were ¥293,643.7 billion at the end of FY2025. Its policy benchmarks are explicitly named: NOMURA-BPI for domestic bonds, FTSE World Government Bond Index for foreign bonds, TOPIX for domestic equities and MSCI ACWI for foreign equities ([GPIF FY2025 results](https://www.gpif.go.jp/en/performance/73509681gpif/gpifannual_report_summary_2025_en.pdf)).

## 3. What they buy and how they allocate capital

### The global allocation pattern

The broad sovereign-fund sample is becoming more diversified, but the diversification is not evenly distributed across institutions.

Invesco’s 2025 study of 75 sovereign wealth funds reported the following allocation pattern:

| Asset category | Share of AUM |
|---|---:|
| Equities | 32% |
| Fixed income | 29% |
| Illiquid alternatives | 23% |
| Liquid alternatives | 4% |
| Direct strategic investments | 9% |

Within its alternative-asset estimates, private equity represented 7.1% of AUM, real estate 7.3%, infrastructure 8.1%, hedge or absolute-return funds 3.1% and commodities 0.8%. These figures are sample estimates using categories that do not necessarily map perfectly onto each other, so they should not be treated as a universal portfolio template ([Invesco Global Sovereign Asset Management Study 2025](https://www.invesco.com/content/dam/invesco/apac/en/pdf/insights/2025/july/invesco-global-sovereign-asset-management-study-2025.pdf)).

State Street Global Advisors reports that private-market allocations in its sample increased from 25% at the end of 2020 to 29% at the end of 2025. It estimates $3.5 trillion of private-market investment in the sample and says private equity accounted for 47% of that category, using “private equity” as a broad catch-all that includes private credit, direct investments, co-investments and club deals. Large funds allocated more to private markets than small funds—30% versus 23%—and less to fixed income—30% versus 38% ([State Street sovereign-fund trends](https://www.ssga.com/us/en/institutional/insights/trends-among-sovereign-wealth-funds)).

The shift has three causes:

1. long-horizon funds can tolerate illiquidity;
2. large funds can support the staffing, due diligence and governance complexity of private investments; and
3. private credit, infrastructure, data centers and real assets offer income or strategic access that public equities alone cannot provide.

The trade-off is that private assets are harder to price, slower to sell, more expensive to manage and more exposed to valuation uncertainty.

### Realized portfolios versus strategic targets

#### Norway and Japan: transparent public-market anchors

The GPFG and GPIF illustrate two different forms of disciplined portfolio construction.

The GPFG’s 2025 realized allocation was 71.3% equities and 26.5% fixed income, with small unlisted real-estate and renewable-infrastructure positions. Its benchmark was 70% equities and 30% fixed income, while its Strategy 25 plan targets a combined listed and unlisted real-estate portfolio of 3–7%. The benchmark and target are not the same as the actual end-period allocation.

GPIF’s target remains 25% in each of four traditional asset classes. Its realized March 2026 allocation was close to target, with 51.39% bonds and 48.61% equities. Its alternatives are classified inside the four traditional categories according to risk-return characteristics rather than reported as an independent strategic bucket. That accounting convention means its 1.74% alternatives share should not be added on top of the four percentages.

GPIF’s portfolio shows why pension funds preserve substantial liquid public-market exposure even while expanding alternatives. Benefits create future cash requirements; the fund therefore needs both return-seeking assets and assets that can be sold or rebalanced efficiently.

#### ADIA: ranges instead of a single allocation

ADIA’s ranges show a deliberately broad generalist portfolio. Even the minimum and maximum ranges do not sum to 100%, because they are fluctuating strategic ranges rather than a single policy portfolio. The fund combines developed and emerging equities, government bonds, credit, hedge funds, managed futures, private equity, real estate, infrastructure and cash.

The 2025 shift toward higher private equity and financial alternatives, alongside a lower real-estate range, indicates rotation within the long-term strategy rather than a simple movement from public to private assets. ADIA said absolute real-estate exposure remained steady.

#### Mubadala: a private-market and strategic-investment blend

Mubadala’s reported portfolio is far more private and strategic than GPFG’s. Its 42% private-market allocation, 17% real estate and infrastructure allocation, 16% alternatives and 5% credit show a portfolio built around direct ownership, partnerships and private-market platforms.

Its asset mix is inseparable from its economic-development role. Energy and infrastructure connect to Abu Dhabi’s industrial base; advanced technology and AI support future-growth ambitions; healthcare and education develop domestic capabilities; and private credit adds cash-yielding exposure that can complement equity investments.

#### PIF: strategic buckets rather than conventional asset classes

PIF’s portfolio buckets separate Saudi equity holdings, sector development, real estate and infrastructure development, giga-projects, international strategic investments, diversified pools, capital-markets programs and Treasury. This is useful for understanding the fund’s policy purpose, but it makes conventional comparisons difficult.

A 29% Saudi Sector Development pool is not equivalent to 29% private equity. It may include operating companies, project finance, infrastructure, equity stakes and state-supported ventures. Likewise, “international strategic investment” may span listed and unlisted assets. The strongest supported conclusion is that PIF allocates by national-development program as much as by financial asset class.

#### CIC, GIC, Temasek, KIA and QIA

CIC discloses its framework and investment types but not a complete percentage allocation across public equities, bonds, private equity, credit, real estate, infrastructure, commodities, hedge funds and cash. The supplied evidence therefore supports a description of its diversified global and private-market platform, not a full actual-versus-target table.

GIC publishes broad asset groups rather than a detailed AUM schedule. Temasek reports portfolio segments rather than conventional asset classes. KIA does not publish a complete actual allocation. QIA describes portfolio construction, direct investment and external-management methods but does not provide a consolidated percentage breakdown. These are unavailable fields, not zero allocations.

### Domestic and foreign exposure

Domestic exposure is one of the sharpest dividing lines between the funds.

| Investor | Domestic or foreign orientation | Evidence and limitation |
|---|---|---|
| GPFG | Almost entirely foreign | NBIM does not invest in Norway as a matter of practice |
| ADIA | Foreign-oriented | ADIA says it does not invest in the UAE as a matter of practice |
| GPIF | Balanced Japan/foreign exposure | March 2026 bonds and equities were divided between domestic and foreign assets; exact overall country totals differ by asset class |
| KIA | Split by fund | FGF invests solely abroad; GRF holds domestic and MENA assets |
| GIC | Global | GIC monitors regional exposure but does not allocate primarily by geography |
| Temasek | Significant Singapore base plus global direct investment | FY2025 segments were 41% Singapore portfolio companies, 36% global direct investments and 23% partnerships/funds |
| Mubadala | Global with a meaningful UAE allocation | Reported geography included 24% UAE and 44% North America |
| PIF | Strongly domestic | Reported domestic share ranges from 76% to 83%, depending on year and reporting basis |
| ADQ | Domestic-leaning | More than one-third of deals in Bloomberg’s sample involved UAE companies |
| QIA | Global with selected domestic and strategic exposure | Actual geographic percentages unavailable |

The classic resource-savings model invests externally to prevent excessive domestic capital inflows, reduce exchange-rate pressure and diversify away from the national economy. The strategic-investment model does the opposite: it deliberately directs capital into domestic infrastructure, companies and sectors.

The OECD distinguishes these roles. Sovereign funds traditionally invest in foreign-currency assets and may hold long-term illiquid assets, while strategic investment funds invest mainly in domestic priority sectors and seek to mobilize private capital. The OECD also warns that domestic investment can expose decisions to political influence unless mandates, benchmarks and safeguards are clear ([OECD strategic investment funds](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2020/06/the-role-of-sovereign-and-strategic-investment-funds-in-the-low-carbon-transition_0321a349/ddfd6a9f-en.pdf)).

### Regional exposure

The funds’ regional patterns reflect both market opportunity and strategic purpose.

The GPFG’s equity exposure is heavily North American because US listed markets are deep, liquid and technologically concentrated. GPIF’s foreign public-market exposure similarly reaches across the United States, Europe and Asia, although its allocation is set through policy benchmarks rather than discretionary geopolitical preferences.

ADIA’s reported geographic ranges place North America first, Europe second, developed Asia third and emerging markets fourth. Mubadala’s reported 2025 geography also placed North America first, but with substantial UAE exposure. PIF’s international allocation is smaller than that of the Gulf’s more globally oriented savings funds because domestic transformation absorbs much of its capital.

KIA’s global reach developed from an early UK base to the United States, Asia-Pacific and emerging markets. QIA’s direct-investment policy is global, with real estate in major cities, private companies, pre-IPO funding and negotiated public-market deals. GIC monitors regional exposure without using geography as its primary allocation framework.

At the level of direct transactions, the broad global pattern became more concentrated in 2024–2025. The IE database counted 391 SWF direct-investment transactions between July 2024 and December 2025, compared with 473 in the previous 18-month window, but aggregate transaction value rose from $211 billion to $404 billion. US targets accounted for 55% of current-window deal value, or $220.4 billion, compared with 31% previously. Because syndicated deal value usually refers to the total transaction rather than the SWF’s individual cheque, these figures measure associated transaction scale rather than exact sovereign capital deployed ([Sovereign Wealth Funds 2026 report](https://www.investinspain.org/content/dam/icex-invest/documentos/publicaciones/publicaciones_eng/swf-2026.pdf)).

### Sector exposure: from finance and real estate to AI and infrastructure

The sector mix has changed as governments have moved from passive ownership of public securities toward direct participation in strategic growth sectors.

In the IE database’s July 2024–December 2025 window, information technology led by deal count with 75 transactions and by associated value with $97.5 billion. Financials recorded 63 deals, healthcare 50, industrials 45 and consumer discretionary 31. Information technology, communication services and real estate together absorbed more than half of total deal value, although the communication-services total was heavily affected by the $55 billion Electronic Arts transaction.

AI-related investments alone represented approximately $118.5 billion of associated deal value across 30 deals, or 29% of the total in that window. The category included frontier-model companies, data centers, compute infrastructure, semiconductors, AI hardware and sovereign-backed application platforms.

The shift is strategic as well as financial:

- QIA and GIC invested in Anthropic;
- MGX participated in OpenAI, xAI, Databricks and data-center platforms;
- PIF developed Humain and AI infrastructure partnerships;
- Mubadala invested in AI infrastructure and technology platforms;
- Temasek invested in quantum computing, software and growth companies;
- GPFG and GIC invested in TenneT Germany and other infrastructure; and
- GPIF and other pension funds expanded infrastructure, private equity and real estate.

Energy investment is also changing. The older model emphasized oil and gas exposure or energy companies. The newer model emphasizes electricity grids, transmission, storage, renewables, data-center power demand and industrial decarbonization. The TenneT transaction, in which GPFG and GIC jointly acquired a minority stake in the German transmission business, illustrates how sovereign capital is moving into regulated infrastructure with long-duration cash flows.

### Direct investment, co-investment and external managers

The implementation method often reveals the institution’s capabilities and risk appetite more clearly than its asset-class labels.

#### Direct investment

Direct investing gives a fund control over the investment decision and, sometimes, influence over operating strategy. It is common at Mubadala, Temasek, PIF, QIA, ADQ and CIC’s private-market subsidiaries.

Direct ownership can support economic-development goals and reduce intermediary fees. It also creates greater concentration, governance demands, valuation uncertainty and political visibility.

#### Co-investment and club deals

Co-investment allows sovereign funds to join a private-equity sponsor or another institutional investor in a specific company or project. It can reduce fees, provide access to specialist due diligence and spread risk across partners.

Mubadala describes typical transactions as meaningful minority co-investments with selected partners. QIA explicitly invests alongside external partners. CIC expanded co-investment platforms, customized accounts and dedicated funds in private markets. GPIF uses co-investment platforms in infrastructure and private equity.

The 2026 IE report counted 23 transactions involving two or more sovereign investors in the July 2024–December 2025 period. Club deals have become normal in AI, digital infrastructure, healthcare, energy and large take-private transactions. They can reduce single-fund concentration, but they may also create correlated exposure if many sovereign funds pursue the same themes.

#### External managers

External managers provide specialist knowledge and access to private-market networks. KIA relies heavily on them; GIC uses them across asset groups; QIA combines internal expertise with external managers; GPIF uses external managers for almost all of its public equities and for fund-of-funds alternatives.

ADIA reported 43% external management in 2025. GPFG’s externally managed mandates amounted to NOK1,062 billion, roughly 5% of its composite value, across 111 equity mandates managed by 103 managers. Its smaller external share reflects its large internal public-market capability.

#### Passive and active management

GPIF provides the clearest distinction. At the end of FY2024, 81.84% of its assets were classified as passive and 17.76% as active. About 90% of its equity investment was in passive funds, but GPIF also used engagement-enhanced passive mandates and active managers seeking excess returns.

“Passive” can mean different things. A fund tracking an ESG index may be passive relative to that ESG index but active relative to the main policy benchmark because its holdings and weights differ. GPIF therefore distinguishes fund-level passive management from whole-portfolio management relative to policy benchmarks.

GPFG manages close to a 70/30 benchmark, but NBIM says all investment processes have active elements. ADIA reported 63% active management and 37% index replication. Temasek does not use a conventional performance benchmark and is mainly active and bottom-up. These differences make labels such as “active” and “passive” meaningful only when the reference benchmark is specified.

### Sovereign capital as catalyst or validator

The rise of sovereign investment in venture capital shows why transaction methods matter.

The IE study examined 1,171 SWF-backed venture deals from 2020–2025. Of these, 220, or 18.8%, involved companies that were later recognized as unicorns. But only 35 deals, or 3%, occurred before the company crossed the $1 billion valuation threshold. The remaining 15.8 percentage points represented investment after the company had already become a recognized winner.

Within the Series A–C and generic venture-stage subset, the pre-unicorn rate rose to 4.7%, roughly within published industry ranges for those stages. The conclusion is not that sovereign funds are uniquely skilled at picking winners. Rather, a small group can invest early enough to behave like venture catalysts, while many larger funds act as validators or late-stage capital providers.

Temasek, GIC and Mubadala accounted for more than 90% of pre-unicorn participations in the dataset. Their common characteristics were internal sector teams, global innovation offices, long-standing venture relationships and the ability to write smaller tickets. ADIA and QIA, by contrast, had a median deal size of $188 million in the dataset, making early-stage investments structurally less practical.

This distinction matters for performance evaluation. A sovereign fund that invests in a mature mega-unicorn may be providing scale, access or strategic positioning rather than demonstrating early-stage selection skill. The same “unicorn exposure” statistic cannot measure both capabilities.

## 4. Why and where governments invest

### Purpose determines portfolio design

The most important relationship in public investment is between purpose, liability and liquidity.

| Objective | Government problem | Typical time horizon | Portfolio implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stabilization | Commodity or fiscal shocks | Short to medium term | Liquid, lower-risk assets |
| Intergenerational savings | Temporary resource wealth | Multi-decade | Global diversification and illiquid assets |
| Pension reserve | Future benefit obligations | Long term, with cash needs | Diversified public markets plus controlled alternatives |
| Reserve investment | Preserve purchasing power | Long term but externally liquid | Foreign bonds, equities and selective alternatives |
| Development | Domestic financing gaps | Long term, project-specific | Infrastructure, private equity and co-investment |
| Industrial or strategic policy | Build national capabilities | Long term, politically shaped | Direct stakes in selected sectors and companies |

Stabilization funds usually maintain more liquid and conservative portfolios because governments may need to draw them at short notice. Savings, reserve-investment and pension funds can accept more illiquidity because their liabilities are longer term. Development funds can accept still greater private-market exposure because their mandate includes domestic investment and market creation ([Sharma background paper](https://www.un.org/esa/ffd/high-level-conference-on-ffd-and-2030-agenda/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2017/11/Background-Paper_Sovereign-Wealth-Funds.pdf)).

### Stabilization and fiscal smoothing

Kuwait’s GRF demonstrates the fiscal role. It receives state proceeds and investment income, helps finance government spending and can smooth fiscal and economic shocks. Ireland’s Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund was designed as a countercyclical buffer and green-investment vehicle, while the Future Ireland Fund was designed for future expenditure pressures.

QIA’s role is also formally multiple: it saves for future generations, supports a competitive Qatari economy and can provide local stabilization. During the 2017–2021 Qatar crisis, the fund reportedly transferred at least $20 billion to the Ministry of Finance at short notice. That case shows how a nominally long-term investment fund can become a national liquidity backstop. The transfer was a reported crisis response, not evidence that all QIA investments are politically directed ([SWP analysis](https://www.swp-berlin.org/en/publication/sovereign-wealth-funds-and-foreign-policy)).

Central-bank and reserve vehicles such as the PBoC, SAFE and MAS have an even stronger liquidity and external-stability function. Their portfolios cannot be evaluated solely by expected long-term return because preserving foreign-exchange capacity and payment-system confidence is part of the mandate.

### Intergenerational savings

Norway’s GPFG and Kuwait’s FGF are the clearest savings vehicles. They convert oil revenue into financial assets and protect future spending capacity after resource income declines.

The investment logic is not simply “maximize return.” It is to preserve purchasing power across generations while maintaining a credible fiscal withdrawal rule. This supports globally diversified portfolios, long horizons and a willingness to accept market volatility.

Norway’s model places unusually strong limits on domestic political use. The fund does not invest in Norway, and the budget uses only the expected real return. Kuwait’s FGF also invests outside Kuwait, although its governance and public disclosure are more restricted.

QIA’s LNG-funded portfolio belongs broadly in this savings tradition, but it has a stronger strategic and domestic-development component than Norway’s GPFG.

### Pension reserves and demographic risk

GPIF invests because Japan’s pension system must manage declining birth rates and population aging. Its reserves are intended to supplement future pension finance, not to finance unrelated industrial policy. The fund’s policy asset mix is determined by long-term pension requirements, expected returns, risk and wage growth.

GPIF’s 2025 policy analysis illustrates the trade-off. A portfolio invested entirely in domestic bonds was modeled to produce a -0.8% real return and a 60.8% lower-partial probability of falling below nominal wage growth. The 25%-each policy mix was modeled to produce a 1.9% real return, 10.34% standard deviation and 42.3% lower-partial probability. The policy mix therefore accepts more short-term volatility to reduce the risk of failing to meet the pension system’s long-term return requirement ([GPIF policy asset mix](https://www.gpif.go.jp/en/15324685gpif/policy_asset_mix_for%20the%205th-term_details.pdf)).

This is not a forecast of realized performance. It is a model-based asset-allocation comparison using assumptions about returns, correlations and economic scenarios.

### Reserve investment and purchasing power

GIC’s objective is to preserve and enhance the international purchasing power of Singapore’s reserves. Its 20-year real-return measure aligns with that mandate. The 65/35 Reference Portfolio is a risk reference, not a return benchmark, because Singapore evaluates GIC against its long-term real-return objective and the risk taken to achieve it.

CIC has a similar reserve-diversification origin but uses a more explicit global portfolio framework. It combines public markets, private markets and direct investment, while Central Huijin separately manages domestic state financial capital.

The reserve-investment model is generally more market-oriented than a development fund. It may invest in strategic sectors, but it does not normally exist to build domestic companies or finance national infrastructure.

### Development, diversification and industrial policy

The development model is most visible in Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi.

PIF’s legal mandate explicitly combines returns with economic development and income diversification. Its domestic-sector pool grew from 4% of the portfolio in 2020 to 30% in 2024, according to Oxford Economics’ review of PIF reporting. Its investments in gaming, tourism, AI, logistics, energy, financial services and giga-projects are intended to change the structure of the Saudi economy.

Mubadala’s domestic role is to create national champions and develop competitive industries. Its international investments provide returns and relationships, while its UAE investments build capabilities in energy, technology, healthcare, education and infrastructure.

ADQ is more concentrated in domestic operating companies and strategic infrastructure. Temasek combines a Singapore holding-company heritage with a global direct-investment model. Its Singapore portfolio companies remain important, but global direct investments have risen substantially over time.

QIA has no single domestic-development pool comparable to PIF’s, but it uses selected domestic investments, local-market partnerships and global strategic transactions to support Qatar’s economic position.

The potential benefit of these models is additionality: public capital can fund projects or sectors that private capital would not finance alone, crowd in foreign investment and build domestic capabilities. The risks are political interference, poor project selection, weak accountability and the possibility that development objectives obscure financial losses.

### Strategic sectors

Four sectors now attract especially strong sovereign interest.

#### Artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure

AI investments are not limited to software companies. Sovereign capital is entering the full stack:

- semiconductors and AI hardware;
- frontier-model companies;
- cloud computing;
- data centers;
- electricity generation and transmission;
- digital networks; and
- sovereign-backed application platforms.

The IE report describes the AI cycle as concentrated among Gulf and Singaporean funds. MGX is the purest example of a single-theme sovereign vehicle, while QIA and GIC have built AI exposure within broader portfolios. PIF is building a domestic AI platform through Humain.

The financial opportunity is large, but so is concentration risk. The biggest AI financings are late-stage, highly valued and often syndicated by the same group of funds. Sovereign investors may provide essential scale, but they may also reinforce valuation pressure and become exposed to the same technology cycle.

#### Energy transition and grids

Energy-transition investment is moving beyond wind and solar generation toward grids, storage, transmission, industrial decarbonization and the power supply required by data centers.

Norway’s GPFG and GIC’s investment in TenneT Germany illustrates the infrastructure model: a long-duration, regulated asset with strategic importance and predictable cash flows. GPIF’s infrastructure portfolio includes power generation, electricity grids, transportation, utilities and telecommunications. Mubadala’s Masdar platform has expanded renewable-energy investment in Spain and other markets.

#### Healthcare and education

Healthcare combines demographic demand with opportunities for private-market growth. ADIA, GIC and Mubadala have invested in healthcare services, medical devices and life sciences.

Mubadala’s investment in Universidad Alfonso X el Sabio in Spain illustrates the expansion of sovereign capital into education. The financial thesis involves stable demand and long-term growth; the strategic thesis includes talent, academic networks and human-capital development.

#### Entertainment, sport and cultural platforms

PIF’s gaming, sports and entertainment investments are unusually integrated with national transformation goals. Its Electronic Arts transaction, Savvy Games Group holdings and investments in media are connected to Saudi Arabia’s effort to develop a global gaming and entertainment sector.

QIA has built a related sports and media platform through interests in sports teams, Formula 1 and broadcasting. These assets may have financial value, but they also carry reputational and geopolitical exposure that is not captured by a conventional return benchmark.

## 5. Governance, transparency and risk

### The Santiago Principles provide a reference, not a uniform rulebook

The Santiago Principles are 24 generally accepted principles for sovereign-fund governance, investment and risk management. They were developed in 2008 by the founding members of the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds. Implementation is voluntary and subordinate to domestic law. The IFSWF emphasizes that the principles are principle-based rather than rules-based, and that member practices are not necessarily comparable ([Santiago Principles](https://www.ifswf.org/santiago-principles)).

The result is a spectrum:

- Norway and GPIF provide extensive public disclosure and formal benchmark information;
- CIC and QIA publish Santiago self-assessments and audited financial information;
- Singapore discloses institutional roles and long-term performance but not GIC AUM or detailed MAS reserve allocations;
- KIA reports to state oversight bodies but restricts public disclosure;
- PIF publishes annual reports and legal documents but its law allows the board to publish its detailed report fully or partially; and
- ADIA does not disclose AUM or holdings.

Transparency is therefore multidimensional. A fund can have audited accounts but not disclose holdings. It can publish asset allocations but not benchmarks. It can be operationally independent while remaining ultimately accountable to a ruler, ministry or parliament.

### Legal mandate and institutional independence

Norway separates political mandate-setting from operational management. The Ministry of Finance and Storting determine the framework, while NBIM implements it. GPFG cannot be used as a discretionary vehicle for political projects outside its mandate.

GPIF’s legal mission is even narrower: manage pension reserves safely and efficiently for the benefit of insured people. Its Board of Governors includes the president and nine external experts. The Board sets the policy asset mix and oversees execution, while an Audit Committee, internal audit, external auditor and multiple risk committees provide oversight.

Singapore’s formal arrangement also separates ownership from investment decisions. The government owns the reserve assets or shares but says it does not direct individual decisions by GIC, MAS or Temasek. Temasek’s board has no government representatives, although the government remains its sole shareholder.

KIA describes its board as fully independent in investment decisions, but the board includes senior government officials and the institution remains embedded in Kuwait’s public-finance system. QIA’s management proposes strategy, its board approves it and the Supreme Council gives ultimate approval. PIF has financial and administrative independence under law but reports to the Council of Economic and Development Affairs, and its board is appointed through royal authority.

The models are not equivalent. “Independence” may mean freedom from day-to-day ministerial instruction, while ultimate ownership and strategic authority remain political.

### Disclosure and accountability

Norway is the outlier in public disclosure. NBIM publishes holdings, voting information, performance, costs and risk measures. It uses GIPS reporting and has independent verification covering 1997–2025. It also discloses its benchmark and tracking error.

GPIF publishes annual reports, holdings by asset category, manager-level data, fees, benchmarks, risk indicators and stewardship activities. It does not select individual equities directly and delegates voting to external managers.

CIC reports audited consolidated statements, a board structure and 12 risk categories, but its self-assessment is institution-produced. QIA reports IFRS financial statements audited by an independent auditor and says performance analysis is available daily to management and regularly to the Board and Supreme Council. However, it does not publish a named consolidated benchmark or complete allocation schedule in the cited material.

KIA submits semiannual AUM statements to the State Audit Bureau and annual accounts to state institutions, but public disclosure is restricted by law. This is a formal accountability system, but it limits external scrutiny.

PIF’s law requires audited statements and an operational report to the Council within 210 days of the fiscal year-end. It does not require that the full report be published. PIF’s reporting has expanded, but its combined development and commercial mandate makes performance attribution more difficult.

A 2022 study of 91 sovereign funds found that sustainability disclosure in 57% of the sample should be substantially enhanced. It found a correlation between fund size and transparency and identified European funds as regional leaders, while cautioning that the evidence on transparency’s effect on national sustainability remained limited ([Cavagnetto et al.](https://doi.org/10.21511/imfi.19(4).2022.18)).

### Benchmarks and performance accountability

A benchmark should tell the public what a fund was expected to achieve and within what risk. The comparison is clearest for GPFG and GPIF.

GPFG has a Ministry of Finance benchmark and a tracking-error limit. GPIF has named policy benchmarks and a policy asset mix tied to pension liabilities. KIA has a three-year rolling objective to exceed composite benchmarks, but the composite benchmark and realized results are not publicly available in the supplied evidence.

CIC reports a 10-year performance target but does not name a conventional market benchmark in the cited passage. ADIA reports long-term time-weighted returns but not a named benchmark. GIC reports a long-term real-return objective and a Policy Portfolio, while explicitly saying its 65/35 Reference Portfolio is not a performance benchmark. Temasek has no conventional reference portfolio. Mubadala reports IRR, while PIF reports annualized returns since 2017 without a benchmark.

This means that “outperformance” cannot be compared across the institutions without knowing:

- whether returns are nominal or real;
- the currency;
- whether fees are deducted;
- whether the measure is time-weighted, money-weighted or total shareholder return;
- the investment horizon;
- whether marks for private assets are provisional; and
- what benchmark or target applies.

### Liquidity risk

Liquidity requirements follow the government’s ability and need to withdraw capital.

GPFG has limited short-term liquidity needs and can hold assets whose value takes a long time to realize. Its cash, fixed-income and listed-equity core supports private real-estate and infrastructure strategies.
